name: Epicatechin
lead: (-)-Epicatechin is a flavan-3-ol, a type of plant polyphenol found in cocoa, green tea, apples, berries and red wine [1][2]. In physique-focused circles it is used as a supplement or via dark chocolate and cocoa powder, on the idea that it supports muscle growth by lowering myostatin (a protein that limits muscle size) and raising follistatin (a protein that opposes myostatin). More muscle mass and a leaner, fuller physique is the appearance goal people attach to it.

The idea traces mainly to a small open-label pilot in seven men with Becker muscular dystrophy, in which muscle biopsies showed higher follistatin and lower myostatin after eight weeks [2][3]. Further registered studies in Becker and Duchenne muscular dystrophy, Friedreich's ataxia and pre-diabetes have been small [4][5][6][7]. Larger human work on cocoa flavanols, which include epicatechin, has examined blood vessel function and cardiovascular outcomes rather than muscle size [8][9]. The Wikipedia catechin article does not discuss muscle effects [1].

chain: Cocoa or tea flavanol taken as food or supplement
Proposed lower myostatin and higher follistatin
Possible easier muscle gain, leaner fuller physique
angle.text: Lifters add cocoa powder, dark chocolate or capsules hoping to push muscle growth by easing the myostatin brake. The muscle-marker data come from patient pilots, so how far this carries to healthy lifters is the open question people discuss.

infobox: Cocoa, tea, apples, berries, red wine [1][2]
EFSA suggests supplement catechins not exceed 800 mg/day [1]

paras: In bodybuilding and strength forums, epicatechin appears in two forms: as food (unsweetened cocoa powder, dark chocolate, tea) and as capsules or powders sold as muscle-support supplements. A T Nation thread about dark chocolate after lifting describes the compound as having suggestive but not conclusive evidence for muscle building, alongside evidence for lower insulin resistance [10]. Other posters list epicatechin in long supplement stacks next to pre-workouts and ursolic acid [11].
Outside fitness, cocoa flavanols are studied for vascular and metabolic health, and tea catechins for general antioxidant effects [8][12].

Epicatechin is the cis form of catechin, with two chiral centres; (-)-epicatechin, the (2R,3R) isomer, is the common natural form [1][2]. Wikipedia reports cocoa as the richest food source in a catechin database, at about 108 mg per 100 g [1]. Grokipedia gives figures such as about 41 to 70 mg per 100 g in dark chocolate, 6 to 15 mg per 100 g in milk chocolate and 6 to 8 mg per 100 ml in brewed green tea, and notes that fermentation and roasting reduce cocoa content [2]. In plants it is built from phenylalanine through the phenylpropanoid pathway [2]. Some forum posters note that alkali-processed cocoa loses much of its epicatechin, and advise choosing natural unsweetened cocoa [13].

Catechins are absorbed mainly in the jejunum and processed in the liver by glucuronidation, sulfation and methylation; most dietary catechins reach the colon, where gut bacteria convert them to smaller compounds. Absorption is highest for (-)-epicatechin among the catechin forms [1]. Because metabolites are extensively transformed, Wikipedia notes the mechanism behind observed vascular effects is not established [1].

Wikipedia's catechin article adds that most dietary catechins are broken down by gut bacteria into gamma-valerolactones and hippuric acids, with only small amounts reaching the blood in modified form, and that (-)-epicatechin is taken up better than (-)-catechin.[1] It also describes the catechins' own antioxidant capacity as low compared with other flavonoids.[1]

Proponents describe a pathway in which epicatechin raises follistatin and lowers myostatin, with effects on mitochondrial biogenesis and muscle regeneration markers [2]. A 2021 review in Nutrition Reviews surveys the compound's reported effects on mitochondria in cells, animals and humans [14]. An earlier study in healthy men reported that (-)-epicatechin accounted for the improvement in flow-mediated dilation seen after flavanol-rich cocoa, linked to nitric oxide [15].

Grokipedia describes an eight-week pilot in seven adult men with Becker muscular dystrophy, in which biopsies showed more mitochondrial and regeneration markers, higher follistatin and lower myostatin [2]. The registration for this pilot lists seven participants and a start in 2013 [3]. Animal work in dystrophy models and aged mice is also cited [2]. The participants were patients rather than healthy lifters, and the pilot had no control group.

Registered trials include the Becker muscular dystrophy pilot (n=7, 2013) [3], a later Becker study (n=2, 2016) [4], a larger Becker biomarker study with (+)-epicatechin (n=22, 2020) [16], a Duchenne muscular dystrophy study in non-ambulatory adolescents (n=15) [5], Friedreich's ataxia (n=10) [6] and two early-phase pre-diabetes studies (n=12 and n=15) [7][17]. A trial in pulmonary arterial hypertension was withdrawn [18], and a study of epicatechin on muscle fat in advanced kidney disease (n=10) was recruiting in 2025 [19].

Among cocoa flavanol trials, the COSMOS randomized trial in older adults tested a cocoa extract supplement for cardiovascular events [8]. An ancillary study reported 2-year effects on epigenetic aging clocks using 500 mg cocoa flavanols per day including 80 mg (-)-epicatechin [9]. A 20-man crossover reported improved flow-mediated dilation, and a trial in obese adults reported no significant change in body measures over 12 weeks [2]. None of these examined muscle size in healthy lifters. Limits across the field include small samples and short durations [2].

Grokipedia states that acute toxicity is low in rodents and that mild gastrointestinal effects have been reported with catechin intakes above about 500 mg a day, drawn from studies of related catechins [2]. Wikipedia notes that green tea extract catechins can be hepatotoxic, that EFSA recommends supplements not exceed 800 mg a day, and that a catechin drug, Catergen, was withdrawn in 1985 after autoimmune haemolytic anaemia [1].

Epicatechin is sold in the US as a dietary supplement. Forum discussion tends to treat cocoa as an inexpensive food source with the compound attached, so many users report adding cocoa to shakes and oats rather than buying capsules [10][13]. Some posts also discuss whether tea or cocoa catechins might influence androgen-related enzymes, citing laboratory work on related tea catechins [20].

Regulators and researchers have examined cocoa flavanols mainly for vascular health. Wikipedia lists a 2006 study linking (-)-epicatechin from flavanol-rich cocoa to vascular effects, a 2012 study reporting lower blood pressure from epicatechin in cocoa products and a 2012 meta-analysis on cocoa and cardiovascular health, while describing the evidence on vasodilation from diet as limited.[1] EFSA called catechins generally safe at normal dietary intake in 2018, and Health Canada published a safety review of green tea extract and liver injury in November 2017.[1]

timeline.event: Freudenberg and colleagues publish on the catechin of cacao bean [1].
Catergen, a catechin-based drug, is withdrawn [1].
A PNAS study in healthy men links (-)-epicatechin to the vascular effects of flavanol-rich cocoa [15].
Becker muscular dystrophy pilot of (-)-epicatechin begins, with seven participants [3].
COSMOS trial reports on cocoa extract and cardiovascular events [8].

lore.intro: Epicatechin is discussed in lifting communities as a food-derived myostatin modulator, usually through cocoa and dark chocolate and sometimes capsules [10][11].

claims.claim: Epicatechin lowers myostatin and raises follistatin, easing muscle gain.
claims.believers: Posters point to the Becker muscular dystrophy pilot and to biopsy changes in follistatin and myostatin, describing the evidence as suggestive for muscle building [10][2].
claims.experts: The pilot had seven patients and no control group; no controlled trial in healthy lifters has been reported [3][2].

claims.claim: Dark chocolate or cocoa powder after training supplies useful epicatechin.
claims.believers: Users add natural cocoa to post-workout meals and note that alkali-processed cocoa loses epicatechin [10][13].
claims.experts: Cocoa is the richest catechin source in food databases, and content falls with fermentation, roasting and processing [1][2].

claims.claim: Epicatechin improves insulin sensitivity and blood flow, which helps training.
claims.believers: Forum posts cite lower insulin resistance and better circulation from cocoa [10].
claims.experts: Cocoa flavanol trials report improved flow-mediated dilation and small blood-pressure changes [2][15], and early-phase pre-diabetes studies have been registered [7].

claims.claim: Tea or cocoa catechins raise testosterone by upregulating enzymes.
claims.believers: A T Nation poster asks about epicatechin upregulating 17beta-HSD3 and cites tea catechin research [21][20].
claims.experts: The cited laboratory work concerns inhibition of 5-alpha-reductase by tea catechin gallates; no human trial of epicatechin on testosterone appears among registered studies [20].

card.summary: Cocoa/tea flavanol marketed as a myostatin inhibitor; evidence is small muscular-dystrophy pilots, not lifters.
card.note: Muscle data come from small patient pilots.

quick.overview:
Epicatechin is a polyphenol in cocoa and tea, sold as a muscle supplement.

The myostatin story rests on a seven-man Becker muscular dystrophy pilot. Controlled trials in healthy lifters were not found.
quick.mechanism: Proponents say it lowers myostatin and raises follistatin; evidence is biopsy markers in a small patient pilot and animal work.
quick.risks: Acute toxicity is low in rodents; mild GI effects are reported at higher catechin intakes. Other catechins (green tea extract) have liver safety concerns.
